case_info.scenario: A 77-year-old woman presented to the ophthalmology department with a 5-year history of a painless neoplasm in her left eye. Her medical history included gastric antral ulcers and reflux esophagitis. She had no history of tumors and no family history of ocular disease. On initial examination, her visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressures were 17 mm Hg in the right eye and 20 mm Hg in the left eye as measured with noncontact tonometry. Pupils were round and reactive, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Slitlamp examination showed an isolated papillary tumor on the limbal conjunctiva, with prominent conjunctival blood vessels extending to the tumor (Figure 1A). The findings of both the anterior segment and fundus examinations were normal. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) demonstrated blood vessels of the neoplasm in the shape of popcorn (Figure 1B) and blood vessels extending beneath the surface of sclera (lower right ofFigure 1A).

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

4. Frustration

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

1. Mental Demand

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

Slitlamp examination showed an isolated papillary tumor on the limbal conjunctiva, with prominent conjunctival blood vessels extending to the tumor (Figure 1A). The findings of both the anterior segment and fundus examinations were normal. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) demonstrated blood vessels of the neoplasm in the shape of popcorn (Figure 1B) and blood vessels extending beneath the surface of sclera (lower right ofFigure 1A).

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.

case_info.caption: A, Slitlamp examination visually showed the neoplasm in the patient’s left eye, and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) showed the shape of tumor vessels (lower right). B, OCTA demonstrated the invasion depth of vessels of this tumor.
case_info.explanation: C. Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is one of the most common types of conjunctival malignant neoplasm arising from stratified squamous epithelium.1,2CSCC usually occurs in middle-aged or older persons, as well as in younger patients with an immunodeficiency.2Clinically, this slow-growing tumor typically appears as a solitary and painless nodule.2This patient presented with a 5-year history of a solitary, slow-growing papillary neoplasm. Conjunctival papilloma (CA) is an acquired benign tumor and generally progresses slowly.3It originates from the stratified squamous epithelium and typically manifests as solitary tissue.4Based on morphology and medical history, it could be relatively difficult to distinguish CSCC from CA in this patient. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva is a particularly aggressive malignant neoplasm with unclear boundaries, composed of both mucus-producing and epidermoid cells.5This lesion has distinct boundaries, making it unlikely to be mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Pathological analysis is usually essential to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Histopathological examination of this patient revealed that a portion of the conjunctival neoplasm was squamous cell carcinoma, while the remainder was papilloma (Figure 2). OCTA examination of the patient demonstrated the depth of invasion of the conjunctival tumor’s blood vessels. Examination indicated that the blood vessels of this tumor might reach sclera, which supported the hypothesis that this might be a malignant tumor. It could be difficult to differentiate CSCC from CA in this case without the results of preoperative OCTA examination. Therefore, OCTA examination could contribute to distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors through the visualization of vessel depth. OCTA can also evaluate the blood supply of ocular-surface abnormalities. Further studies are needed to explore the accuracy of OCTA for the diagnosis of ocular surface disease. Complete surgical excision is warranted for therapy of conjunctival tumors. CSCC confers a risk of recurrence and metastasis. Considering the high recurrence rates, adjuvant therapies are commonly used, and these therapies could augment surgical excision in patients with CSCC.6Adjunctive treatments mainly include cryotherapy, topical mitomycin therapy, conjunctival autograft, and radiotherapy.7 Observation and periodic review (choice A) might be an option when the neoplasm is small, in its early stages. This tumor is relatively large; therefore continued observation without treatment is probably not appropriate. Surgical excision with conjunctival autograft (choice B) would be insufficient for this patient, considering the depth of the invasion of the vessels observed on OCTA and biopsy results. Surgical excision with radiotherapy (choice D) would not be preferred because radiotherapy might induce various complications, which may persist in the long term and would decrease quality of life.6Surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy (choice C) is recommended, as it has been documented to have an excellent prognosis in these situations.8Adjunctive use of mitomycin could reduce the prevalence of recurrences compared with no adjunctive therapy (5.9% vs 66.7%).9However, mitomycin therapy may be accompanied by irritative symptoms. This patient underwent complete surgical excision with topical mitomycin therapy. At a follow-up visit 1 month after surgery, there was no ocular recurrence or systemic metastasis.
